pages.title: WELCOME TO NORMAN ROOTS
content: Catch. Carry. Change. Uncle. Cousin. Flower.
River. City. Peace. These feel like the most
English words in English. They are French:
every one arrived with the Normans in 1066
and quietly refused to leave.
For three hundred years the court spoke
French and the farm spoke English. When the
two fused, English kept both: begin and
commence, ask and demand, cow and beef,
house and mansion. One word from each layer,
side by side, never quite the same.
This pack teaches the French layer, a
thousand words, and on every card the two
words that stand beside it. You need no
French. You need to notice.

pages.title: HOW A CARD WORKS
content: The front shows a word. Press a key and the
card opens in stages: a sentence that uses
it, its DEFINITION, a second example built
on a TWIN of the word, and, on 8, the notes.
The notes name where the word came from and
its two neighbours: the GERMANIC twin, the
plain English word that means the same
(catch beside grab), and the LATIN twin,
the same Latin root taken straight from
Latin (catch beside capture). The Norman
word is the bridge between the two.
Rate the card 0 to 5 when it is open. The
boss fight asks the definition and offers
eight words; the synonyms and antonyms in
the notes are the clues you take with you.
TIER 1 is the everyday French: the verbs,
the things, the people, the wide world and
the plain adjectives that nobody thinks of
as French at all.
TIER 2 is the Norman domains: law, the
court, war, the kitchen, the church, the
house. TIER 3 is the register shift, where
commence outranks begin. TIER 4 is the
machinery: the suffixes and the sound splits
(ward and guard). TIER 5 is the French that
hides in plain sight, and the French that
never hid at all.
Every cluster opens with a short lesson
naming its words.
THE NEXT 23 CARDS: catch, carry, change.
The second set of everyday verbs. Not one
of them looks French, and every one is.
Each came in on top of a plain English
word that was already doing the work.
arrive    beside the older come
finish    beside the older end
demand    beside the plain ask
repair    beside stitch
The French word is usually the longer
one, and the longer one is the one that
sounds careful. Ask and demand are the
same act with different manners.
THE NEXT 22 CARDS: verbs of every day.
Nouns so ordinary that nothing marks them
out: the air, a chair, a page, a plate.
Every one is French, and every one has an
English word still standing beside it.
art      beside the older craft
chair    beside the plain seat
page     beside the older leaf
plate    beside the older dish
Craft kept the skill in it and art took
the beauty. A leaf belongs to a tree and
to a book alike; page took the book and
left the tree alone.
THE NEXT 22 CARDS: the names of things.
Weights, prices, letters, maps. These are
the words of trade and of paperwork, and
all of them came in from French.
price     beside the older worth
table     beside the older board
letter    beside the older writ
route     beside the plain way
A board is still the plank a table is
made of, and a man still boards with the
family whose table he eats at. The older
word survives in the corners of the new.
THE NEXT 24 CARDS: trade and record.
Mother, father, brother and sister are
English to the bone. Aunt, uncle and
cousin came in with the Normans. The
house inside stayed English; the family
beyond it took French names, and so did
most of the people met outside the door.
aunt   beside the plain kinswoman
uncle  beside the plain kinsman
enemy  beside the older foe
people beside the older folk
Foe has gone stiff and poetic and enemy
does the plain daily work, which is the
reverse of the usual arrangement.
THE NEXT 23 CARDS: names for people.
Rivers, flowers, cities, forests. The
land was English and half the words for
it are French: the Normans named the
wide world over the top of the old
names, and both sets are still in use.
river     beside the older stream
city      beside the older town
flower    beside the older bloom
forest    beside the older wood
A forest was not simply trees. It was
land kept for the king's hunting under
its own French law, while a wood was
only a wood.
THE NEXT 22 CARDS: the world outside.
Adjectives that feel as English as any:
large, clear, safe, plain. All French,
each with an older word beside it.
large     beside the blunt big
brief     beside the plain short
safe      beside the older sound
tender    beside the plain soft
Safe and sound is the pair caught in one
phrase, the French word and the English
word saying it twice over.
Very is French as well. It once meant
true, and it has crowded out the old
full, which survives in full well.
THE NEXT 22 CARDS: plain adjectives.
More of the plain adjectives, and one of
them pushed a native word out of its job.
real    beside the older true
fine    beside the plain good
just    beside the older fair
vast    beside the older wide
Old English counted first, other, third.
Second is French, and it took the place
of other so completely that other now
means only the one that is left.
Good and fine are not one offer: a fine
meal is a good meal with a price on it.
That is the French word's usual work.
THE NEXT 22 CARDS: more adjectives.
Here the French layer took the field
almost whole. Beauty, danger, justice,
mercy, honor: the words for what cannot
be touched are nearly all French.
joy      beside the older bliss
peace    beside the older rest
mercy    beside the older ruth
force    beside the older might
The English words did not all survive.
Ruth, the native word for mercy, is all
but gone. It still does its work inside
ruthless, where nobody notices it.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: things you cannot see.
The second run of abstracts: what is
felt, what is owed and what is risked.
rage    beside the older wrath
pain    beside the older ache
wage    beside the older hire
debt    beside the older score
Debt arrived from French as dette. The
b was put in later by scribes who knew
the Latin debitum and wanted it seen.
Nobody has ever pronounced it.
Law came in from Old Norse and rule from
French. Each set of newcomers left
English a word for what is laid down.
THE NEXT 23 CARDS: pleasure and debt.
